short: A loan, usually floating-rate and secured on the company's assets, made to a borrower that already carries heavy debt or has a low credit rating.
kid: Imagine a friend who already owes lots of sweets to other kids and asks you for more. You might still lend, but you ask for extra sweets back and keep his best toy until he pays.
detail: A leveraged loan is a loan to a company that is already heavily indebted, typically one rated below investment grade (BB+ or lower) or carrying debt of more than about four to five times EBITDA. Most are senior secured term loans arranged by banks and then sold to institutional investors such as CLOs, loan funds and private credit funds. They pay a floating rate, a benchmark like SOFR plus a credit spread, so the borrower's interest bill rises when rates rise. Leveraged loans fund buyouts, acquisitions and dividend recapitalisations, and their market is a key gauge of risk appetite. Do not confuse them with high-yield bonds: both go to junk-rated companies, but loans are usually secured, floating-rate and repayable early, while bonds are typically unsecured and fixed-rate. In India, buyouts have leaned more on NBFCs, private credit and offshore loans because banks were long restricted from funding share acquisitions.
example: Say XYZ Ltd, with EBITDA of $100 million, takes a $500 million leveraged loan at a benchmark rate plus 3.5%. If the benchmark is, say, 4%, the loan costs 7.5%, or $37.5 million a year. Its leverage is 5 times EBITDA and its interest cover is about 2.7 times ($100 million / $37.5 million).
formula: Loan rate = Floating benchmark (e.g. SOFR) + Credit spread; Leverage = Total debt / EBITDA

short: Loans made directly to companies by investment funds rather than banks, negotiated privately and usually held until repaid instead of being traded.
kid: Sometimes a friend needs to borrow toys and the toy shop says no. So a rich uncle lends the toys himself, and asks for a few extra toys back for helping.
detail: Private credit is lending by non-bank investors, mainly funds raised from pension funds, insurers and wealthy families, directly to companies. The largest slice is direct lending to mid-sized firms, often owned by private equity, but the term also covers mezzanine, distressed and special-situations debt. Loans are negotiated one-to-one, are usually floating-rate, carry tight covenants and pay more than bank loans or bonds in return for illiquidity and speed. The market grew to well over a trillion dollars globally by the mid-2020s as banks retreated after 2008 under stricter capital rules. Supporters say it fills a funding gap; critics worry about opaque valuations, rising leverage and hidden links back to banks. In India, private credit flows mostly through Category II alternative investment funds and offshore funds, financing real estate, promoters and companies that banks avoid. Do not confuse private credit, which lends, with private equity, which buys ownership.
example: Say a private credit fund lends ₹200 crore to ABC Ltd for four years at 13% a year plus a 1% upfront fee. ABC pays ₹26 crore of interest each year and ₹2 crore of fees at the start, so over four years the fund earns ₹106 crore before any losses.

short: Bonds or loans of a company that has defaulted or is close to it, trading far below their face value.
kid: A friend broke his toy and promised to give you a new one, but he might not manage it. Someone could buy that promise from you for one sweet, hoping to get the whole toy later.
detail: Distressed debt means bonds and loans of borrowers that are in default, in bankruptcy, or likely to get there. A common rule of thumb treats a bond as distressed when its yield is more than 10 percentage points (1,000 basis points) above government bonds, or when it trades below about 70 to 80 percent of face value. Specialist investors buy such debt cheaply, betting that the eventual recovery will beat the price paid; some aim to swap their claims for control of the company, a strategy called loan-to-own. Returns depend heavily on legal rights, seniority and the speed of the bankruptcy process. In India, asset reconstruction companies and special-situations funds buy stressed loans from banks, often resolving them through the IBC. The common confusion: distressed does not mean worthless. The price already reflects heavy expected losses, so the debt can still be a good buy.
example: Say XYZ Ltd's bonds with a face value of ₹100 trade at ₹40 after it defaults. If the resolution pays ₹60 per bond, the buyer gains ₹20 on ₹40, a 50% return; if it pays only ₹25, the buyer loses ₹15, or 37.5%.
formula: Return on distressed purchase = (Recovery value - Purchase price) / Purchase price

short: An investor, often a hedge fund, that buys defaulted debt very cheaply and then pushes hard, sometimes in court, to be repaid in full.
kid: A friend could not give back all the marbles he owed. Most kids said 'just give us half', but one kid bought the others' promises cheaply and kept asking for every single marble.
detail: Vulture fund is a critical nickname for investors who buy the debt of struggling companies or governments at deep discounts and then hold out for much more than other creditors accept, often by suing. The tactic is best known in sovereign debt: Elliott Management's long legal fight over defaulted Argentine bonds ended in a 2016 settlement that paid holdout creditors billions of dollars. Critics say such funds profit from the distress of poor countries and block orderly restructurings; the UK passed a law in 2010 limiting what they can recover from heavily indebted poor countries. Defenders argue that they give original lenders an exit, make markets for unloved debt and enforce contracts. The confusion to avoid: not every distressed debt investor is a vulture. The term applies mainly to aggressive holdout litigation, not to funds that buy cheap debt and then join a negotiated restructuring.
example: Say a fund buys $100 million (face value) of a country's defaulted bonds for $20 million. Other creditors accept a deal paying 30 cents per dollar, which would give the fund $30 million, a 50% gain. If it holds out and wins the full $100 million in court, it makes five times its money.

short: A deal in which lenders cancel some or all of a company's debt and take new shares in the company instead.
kid: You lent your friend ten toy cars for his lemonade stand, but he cannot give them back. Instead, he makes you part-owner of the stand, so you share the lemonade money.
detail: In a debt-for-equity swap, creditors give up their claim to be repaid and receive shares in the borrower instead. It is a standard restructuring tool when a company's debt is more than its business can carry: interest costs fall, the balance sheet deleverages, and creditors gain upside if the business recovers. The price is dilution, because existing shareholders end up owning a smaller slice, sometimes almost nothing. India's RBI tried it through the Strategic Debt Restructuring scheme of 2015, letting banks convert loans into a majority stake, but few cases found new owners and the scheme was withdrawn in 2018 in favour of the IBC. In 2023 the Indian government became Vodafone Idea's largest shareholder after converting about ₹16,000 crore of interest it was owed on deferred spectrum and AGR dues into equity. Do not confuse this with a convertible bond, where the right to convert is agreed at issue.
example: Say ABC Ltd owes ₹500 crore and has 10 crore shares. Lenders convert ₹200 crore of debt into new shares at ₹20 each, receiving 10 crore shares. ABC now has ₹300 crore of debt and 20 crore shares, and the lenders own 50% of the company.
formula: New shares issued = Debt converted / Conversion price per share

short: Any extra protection added to a loan or bond, such as a guarantee or extra collateral, so lenders face less risk and charge less.
kid: You want to borrow a ball, but your friend is unsure you will return it. Your big sister promises she will give it back if you don't, so your friend happily lends it.
detail: Credit enhancement is any feature that lowers the risk of a debt instrument, so it earns a higher credit rating and a lower interest rate than the borrower could get alone. Internal enhancement is built into the structure: subordination (junior tranches absorb losses first), over-collateralisation (more assets than debt), cash reserves and excess spread. External enhancement comes from a third party: a bank guarantee, a letter of credit, bond insurance (a credit wrap) or a partial credit guarantee from a development lender. It is central to securitisation. In India, RBI lets banks offer partial credit enhancement to corporate bonds, and SEBI rules as of 2025 require ratings resting on third-party support to carry a CE suffix, such as AA (CE), so investors can see the rating is borrowed. The common mistake is to treat an enhanced rating as the issuer's own strength: if the guarantor weakens, the rating falls too.
example: Say ABC Ltd alone would be rated BBB and pay 11% on ₹100 crore of bonds. A bank guarantees ₹40 crore of the issue for a fee of 0.75% a year on that ₹40 crore, the bonds are rated AA (CE) and pay 9%. Interest falls by ₹2 crore a year, the fee costs ₹30 lakh, so ABC saves ₹1.7 crore a year.

short: When a person or company cannot pay its debts as they fall due, or owes more than everything it owns is worth.
kid: You promised your friends ten sweets, but your jar only has four and you can't get more. You are stuck, and you can't keep your promise.
detail: Insolvency is the financial condition of being unable to meet debts. There are two tests. Cash-flow insolvency means a borrower cannot pay what is due when it is due. Balance-sheet insolvency means total liabilities exceed total assets, so net worth is negative. A company can fail one test and pass the other: a firm with valuable factories but no cash can be cash-flow insolvent, while a firm with negative net worth can keep paying for years if lenders keep rolling over its loans. Insolvency is a state; bankruptcy and insolvency proceedings are the legal processes that follow. In India, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code lets a creditor start proceedings once a company defaults above a threshold, without proving balance-sheet insolvency. A common confusion is with illiquidity: an illiquid firm is short of cash for now but solvent, and can survive with a short-term loan.
example: Say ABC Ltd owns assets worth ₹80 crore but owes ₹100 crore, so its net worth is minus ₹20 crore: it is balance-sheet insolvent. If it also has ₹10 crore of loan repayments due this month but only ₹4 crore in cash and no lender willing to help, it is cash-flow insolvent too.
formula: Net worth = Total assets - Total liabilities (a negative figure signals balance-sheet insolvency)

short: A court-supervised legal process for a person or company that cannot pay its debts, ending in either a rescue plan or a sale of assets.
kid: When someone can't give back what they borrowed, a grown-up referee steps in. The referee shares out what is left fairly, or helps them start again.
detail: Bankruptcy is the legal procedure that deals with insolvency. Once a debtor files, or creditors force it in, a court or tribunal takes charge: creditors are usually stopped from grabbing assets individually, claims are collected and checked, and the debtor is either reorganised under a plan or liquidated, with the proceeds shared out in order of priority. In the US, Chapter 11 is for reorganisation and Chapter 7 for liquidation. Lehman Brothers' filing in September 2008, with over $600 billion of assets, is the largest in US history. In India, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code uses bankruptcy mainly for individuals and partnership firms, while companies go through the corporate insolvency resolution process. The common confusion is that bankrupt means closed: many companies keep operating through bankruptcy and emerge with less debt, though shareholders are often wiped out.
example: Say a company owes $500 million and its assets fetch $200 million in a bankruptcy sale. After $20 million of legal and administrative costs, creditors share $180 million, a recovery of 36 cents per dollar owed.
formula: Recovery rate = Amount recovered by creditors / Total claims

short: Closing down a company by selling everything it owns and paying its debts in a fixed order, after which the company ceases to exist.
kid: When a lemonade stand closes for good, you sell the jug, the table and the cups. The money goes to the people the stand owes, and then the stand is gone.
detail: Liquidation, also called winding up, ends a company's life. A liquidator takes control, sells the assets, either piecemeal or as a going concern, and distributes the cash to claimants in a legal order of priority, with shareholders last. Under India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, NCLT orders liquidation when no resolution plan is approved in time or the creditors vote for it; proceeds then follow the Section 53 waterfall. Solvent companies can also liquidate voluntarily. IBBI data as of 2025 showed that more insolvency cases have ended in liquidation than in resolution plans, though many were already defunct businesses, and resolution plans recover far more value. Liquidation value, what the assets fetch in a forced sale, is usually much lower than going-concern value, which is why creditors prefer a rescue. Do not confuse this with liquidation in trading, which means closing out positions, often forced by margin calls.
example: Say XYZ Ltd's assets sell for ₹150 crore and liquidation costs take ₹10 crore. Ignoring workmen's dues for simplicity, secured lenders owed ₹200 crore receive the remaining ₹140 crore, a 70% recovery, while unsecured creditors and shareholders get nothing.

short: India's 2016 law giving creditors a time-bound process to rescue a defaulting company or, failing that, close it and sell its assets.
kid: When someone can't give back what they borrowed, there is a clear rulebook. Everyone who lent gets together, picks a helper, and has a fixed time to fix things or share out what is left.
detail: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) replaced a tangle of slow laws with one framework for corporate, partnership and individual insolvency. When a company defaults, a financial creditor (Section 7), an operational creditor (Section 9) or the company itself (Section 10) can apply to NCLT. Once a case is admitted, a moratorium halts lawsuits, the board is suspended, a resolution professional runs the company, and a committee of financial creditors decides its fate within 180 days, extendable to an outer limit of 330 days including litigation. Section 29A bars defaulting promoters from buying back their companies. The shift to creditor-in-control changed behaviour: many promoters now settle before admission. Under the rules as of 2025, the minimum default is ₹1 crore; by then resolution plans had recovered roughly a third of admitted claims on average. Common confusion: the IBC is meant to resolve companies, not simply to recover dues.
example: Say a bank is owed ₹5 crore by ABC Ltd, which has defaulted. Because the default is above the ₹1 crore threshold under the rules as of 2025, the bank can apply to NCLT. If the approved resolution plan pays it ₹2 crore, the bank recovers 40% and takes a 60% haircut.

short: India's special court-like body for company law disputes and corporate insolvency cases; appeals go to an appellate tribunal, then the Supreme Court.
kid: When grown-ups who run shops argue about money, they go to a special judge. This judge only listens to shop problems and decides who is right.
detail: The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) is a quasi-judicial body set up in 2016 under the Companies Act, 2013. It is the adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency under the IBC: it admits or rejects insolvency applications, appoints the interim resolution professional, approves resolution plans and orders liquidation. It also handles mergers and demergers, oppression and mismanagement cases and other company law matters that earlier sat with high courts and the Company Law Board. NCLT sits in benches across major cities. Its orders can be appealed to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) and then to the Supreme Court. For markets, NCLT hearings and orders move the share and bond prices of stressed companies. A known problem is backlog: admission and approval often take far longer than the IBC intends. Do not confuse NCLT with Debt Recovery Tribunals, which hear bank recovery suits and personal insolvency.
example: Say a lender files an insolvency petition against ABC Ltd. The IBC asks NCLT to decide on admission within 14 days, but suppose it takes 120 days. Since the 330-day outer limit runs from admission, the process is meant to end within 450 days of filing, though many cases run longer.

short: The step-by-step process under India's insolvency law where creditors take charge of a defaulting company and try to find a buyer or rescue plan.
kid: When a lemonade stand can't pay back its friends, the friends take over for a while. They look for someone kind and clever to buy the stand and keep it running.
detail: The corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) is the rescue stage of India's IBC. It starts when NCLT admits an application from a creditor or the company. A moratorium then freezes lawsuits and asset seizures, the board's powers pass to an interim resolution professional, and claims are invited. A committee of financial creditors (CoC) is formed, and the resolution professional runs the business as a going concern, appoints valuers and invites resolution plans from bidders. A plan approved by 66% of the CoC's vote goes to NCLT for final approval; if none is approved in time, the company is liquidated. The law sets 180 days, extendable by 90, with an outer limit of 330 days including litigation, though many cases run much longer. Common confusion: admission into CIRP is not liquidation. The aim is to keep the company alive under new owners, and its plants usually keep running throughout.
example: Say ABC Ltd enters CIRP with admitted claims of ₹2,000 crore. The best resolution plan offers ₹600 crore, so creditors recover 30% and take a 70% haircut. If no plan had passed by day 330, ABC would have gone into liquidation.

short: A bidder's proposal, approved by creditors and the tribunal, to take over and revive a company in India's insolvency process, stating each creditor's payout.
kid: A broken toy shop needs a new owner. Someone writes a plan saying 'I will fix the shop and give everyone back some of their toys', and if the friends agree, the plan wins.
detail: A resolution plan is the rescue proposal submitted by a resolution applicant, the bidder, during a CIRP. It sets out how much each class of creditor will be paid, in cash, new debt or equity, and how the business will be funded. To be valid it must pay insolvency costs first, give operational creditors and dissenting financial creditors at least what they would get in liquidation, and come from a bidder eligible under Section 29A, which bars wilful defaulters and promoters of defaulting firms. It needs at least 66% of the committee of creditors' vote and then NCLT approval, after which it binds everyone and extinguishes claims not included, the clean slate principle. ArcelorMittal's roughly ₹42,000 crore takeover of Essar Steel, cleared by the Supreme Court in 2019, is a landmark case. Do not confuse the highest bid with the best plan: creditors also weigh upfront cash, feasibility and timing.
example: Say ABC Ltd has admitted claims of ₹1,000 crore and a liquidation value of ₹250 crore. A plan paying ₹450 crore gives creditors a 45% recovery, a 55% haircut, but 1.8 times what liquidation would fetch, so the committee of creditors approves it.
formula: Recovery under plan = Plan payout / Admitted claims

short: A licensed insolvency expert who takes charge of a defaulting company during India's insolvency process, runs it, gathers creditor claims and invites rescue bids.
kid: When a lemonade stand gets into trouble, a careful helper is picked to look after it. The helper keeps the stand open, writes down who is owed what, and finds someone to buy it.
detail: A resolution professional (RP) is an insolvency professional registered with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) who manages a company during its CIRP. On admitting a case, NCLT appoints an interim resolution professional (IRP), who takes over from the suspended board, makes a public announcement, collects and verifies claims and forms the committee of creditors. The CoC can confirm the IRP as RP or replace them with a 66% vote. The RP then runs the company as a going concern, appoints valuers, prepares an information memorandum for bidders, checks resolution plans for legal compliance and puts them to a CoC vote. Their fees and costs are paid first from any recovery. The common confusion is about power: the RP is a manager and process-keeper, not a judge, and does not decide which plan wins. That is the CoC's commercial call, subject to NCLT approval.
example: Say NCLT admits ABC Ltd and names an IRP; at the first meeting, lenders holding 70% of the votes choose a different RP, clearing the 66% bar. If the RP's fee is ₹15 lakh a month and the process takes 9 months, fees total ₹1.35 crore, paid ahead of creditors as process costs.

short: The group of lenders to a company in India's insolvency process that votes on its future, with votes weighted by how much each is owed.
kid: Everyone who lent toys to a friend sits in a circle to decide what happens next. The kid who lent the most toys gets the loudest voice.
detail: The committee of creditors (CoC) is the decision-making body in a CIRP. It is made up of financial creditors, those who lent money such as banks, NBFCs, bondholders and homebuyers, excluding any related to the company. Each member votes in proportion to its admitted financial debt. Key decisions, including approving a resolution plan, replacing the resolution professional and extending the timeline, need 66% of the vote; routine matters need 51%. Operational creditors such as suppliers do not vote, though larger ones can attend meetings. In the Essar Steel judgment of 2019, the Supreme Court held that courts should not second-guess the commercial wisdom of the CoC. This makes the IBC creditor-in-control, unlike US Chapter 11, where management usually keeps running the company. A common confusion: the CoC does not include every creditor, and a single big bank can hold an effective veto.
example: Say Bank A is owed ₹500 crore, Bank B ₹300 crore and Fund C ₹200 crore, so the CoC has ₹1,000 crore of votes. A plan backed by A and B gets 80% and passes. A plan backed by B and C gets only 50% and fails, so Bank A, with 50%, can block any plan.
formula: Voting share = Creditor's admitted financial debt / Total admitted financial debt

short: The share of what they are owed that lenders agree to give up when a borrower cannot repay in full.
kid: You lent your friend ten crayons, but he can only give back four. You say 'that's okay, keep the rest', and the six you let go are the haircut.
detail: In credit, a haircut is the loss creditors accept in a restructuring, settlement or insolvency, expressed as a percentage of their claim. If lenders owed ₹100 receive ₹30, the haircut is 70%. Haircuts are the headline number in Indian IBC cases, where some large resolutions have involved haircuts above 90%, and in sovereign restructurings: private holders of Greek government bonds took a face-value haircut of about 53.5% in 2012. Recovery rate is the flip side: recovery plus haircut equals 100%. The word has a second meaning in secured lending and repo markets, where a haircut is the cut applied to collateral's market value before lending against it, a safety margin rather than a loss; a lender might advance only ₹95 against a bond worth ₹100. Read headlines carefully: a big haircut is not automatically a bad deal if liquidation would have recovered even less.
example: Say lenders are owed ₹1,000 crore and accept ₹350 crore under a resolution plan. The haircut is (1,000 - 350) / 1,000 = 65%, and the recovery is 35%.
formula: Haircut = (Amount owed - Amount recovered) / Amount owed x 100

short: An insolvency route where a company and its main lenders agree a rescue plan first, then file it for quick court approval.
kid: Before asking the teacher for help, two friends sit down and agree how to share out the broken toys fairly. Then the teacher just checks it and says yes.
detail: In a pre-packaged insolvency, the debtor negotiates a resolution plan with its main financial creditors before entering formal proceedings, so the court-supervised part is short and cheap. India added the pre-packaged insolvency resolution process (PPIRP) to the IBC in 2021, for MSMEs only. Under the rules as of 2025, it needs a default of at least ₹10 lakh, approval from unrelated financial creditors holding at least 66% of financial debt before filing, and a base resolution plan from the existing owners. Unlike a regular CIRP, management usually stays in control (debtor-in-possession), and the process must finish within 120 days. If the plan impairs operational creditors, it must face a Swiss challenge, letting outside bidders try to beat it. As of 2025, uptake had been very low, with only a handful of admissions. The idea is borrowed from prepackaged Chapter 11 filings in the US and pre-pack administrations in the UK.
example: Say ABC MSME Pvt Ltd owes its lenders ₹8 crore. Before filing, lenders holding ₹6 crore (75% of the debt, above the 66% bar) agree a plan paying ₹4.8 crore in total. Once NCLT approves, creditors recover 60% overall and the company keeps operating.

short: Specialised Indian tribunals where banks and financial institutions go to recover large unpaid loans faster than through ordinary civil courts.
kid: When a friend won't give back a big pile of borrowed toys, the lender can go to a special helper who only sorts out borrowing fights. That helper can make the friend hand things back.
detail: Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRTs) were set up under the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, now the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, to speed up loan recovery that used to take years in civil courts. Under the rules as of 2025, banks and financial institutions can file claims of ₹20 lakh or more. A DRT issues a recovery certificate, and its recovery officers can attach and auction the borrower's property. Borrowers also go to the DRT to challenge a bank's actions under the SARFAESI Act, and under the IBC it is the adjudicating authority for insolvency of individuals and partnership firms. Appeals lie with the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT). Heavy backlogs mean cases often outlast their intended timelines. Do not confuse DRT with NCLT: a DRT is mainly about recovering a loan, NCLT about resolving a whole company.
example: Say a bank is owed ₹50 lakh by a trader who has stopped paying. The DRT issues a recovery certificate for that amount, and the recovery officer auctions the trader's shop for ₹42 lakh. The bank recovers 84% of its claim before interest and costs.

short: The part of US bankruptcy law that lets a struggling company keep operating while it reorganises its debts under court protection.
kid: A shop owes too many people money. A judge says 'stop chasing the shopkeeper for a while', so the shop stays open and works out a fair plan to pay people back.
detail: Chapter 11 of the US Bankruptcy Code governs corporate reorganisation. When a company files, an automatic stay stops creditors from suing or seizing assets, and management usually stays in charge as debtor-in-possession. The company can raise new DIP financing that ranks ahead of older debt, reject unprofitable contracts and propose a plan of reorganisation, which creditors vote on by class before the court confirms it. A court can cram down a plan on a dissenting class if it is fair and equitable. Shareholders are often wiped out and creditors become the new owners. General Motors went through Chapter 11 in 2009 and emerged in about 40 days. Chapter 7, by contrast, is liquidation: a trustee sells the assets and the business shuts. The key contrast with India's IBC is control: in Chapter 11 the debtor's managers run the process, while under the IBC creditors and a resolution professional take charge.
example: Say XYZ Inc owes $800 million to secured lenders and $200 million to bondholders, and the reorganised business is worth $900 million. The plan gives secured lenders $600 million of new debt plus two-thirds of the new equity, worth $200 million, so they recover in full. Bondholders get the other third, $100 million or 50 cents per dollar, and old shareholders get nothing.

short: Bundling many loans, such as home or car loans, and selling them to a separate entity that issues securities paid from those loans' repayments.
kid: A lemonade stand is owed small coins by lots of friends. It puts all those promises in one box and sells the box to someone, who gets the coins as the friends pay.
detail: Securitisation turns a pool of illiquid loans or receivables into tradable securities. The originator, say a bank or NBFC, sells the loans to a special purpose vehicle, which pays for them by issuing securities to investors; borrowers' repayments then flow through to those investors, usually in tranches of different seniority. The originator gets cash to lend again, frees up capital and moves some risk off its books, while investors gain access to diversified loan pools. In India, RBI's 2021 directions on securitisation of standard assets set minimum holding periods and require originators to keep some exposure, so they still care about loan quality. Most Indian deals use pass-through certificates or direct assignment of loans. Securitisation of US subprime mortgages was at the heart of the 2008 crisis. Do not confuse it with the SARFAESI Act's use of the word, which concerns asset reconstruction companies buying bad loans.
example: Say ABC Finance pools 10,000 vehicle loans worth ₹500 crore and sells them to a trust. The trust issues ₹450 crore of senior certificates to investors and ₹50 crore of junior certificates that ABC keeps. ABC gets ₹450 crore of fresh cash and retains 10% of the risk.

short: A separate company or trust set up for one narrow job, such as holding a loan pool or a project, to isolate its risks.
kid: You keep your birthday money in a special box, apart from your pocket money. If you lose the pocket money, the birthday box is still safe.
detail: A special purpose vehicle (SPV), or special purpose entity, is a legal entity created for a single, limited purpose and designed to be bankruptcy-remote, meaning the troubles of its sponsor should not reach its assets, and vice versa. In securitisation, the SPV, usually a trust in India, buys the loans and issues securities to investors. In project finance, a road, power plant or airport sits in its own SPV so lenders can rely on the project's cash flows alone. SPVs also hold assets under InvITs and REITs and are used in joint ventures and acquisitions. Used badly, they can hide debt: Enron's collapse in 2001 involved off-balance-sheet entities that concealed liabilities. The common mistake is assuming an SPV is automatically off the sponsor's balance sheet; under accounting standards such as Ind AS 110, a sponsor that controls the SPV must consolidate it.
example: Say a sponsor builds a ₹1,000 crore toll road through an SPV funded with ₹700 crore of loans and ₹300 crore of its own equity. If traffic disappoints and the SPV fails, lenders can generally claim only the road's tolls and assets, so the sponsor's maximum loss is its ₹300 crore.

short: One slice of a larger loan or bond deal, with its own risk, return or timing; senior slices are paid first, junior slices lose first.
kid: Picture friends lined up for sweets from one bag. The first in line always gets his share. The last in line might miss out if the bag runs short, so he is promised a bigger handful.
detail: Tranche, French for slice, is a portion of a financing with its own terms. In securitisations, CDOs and CLOs, a pool of loans backs several tranches stacked by seniority: the senior tranche is paid first and gets the highest rating and lowest yield; mezzanine tranches sit in the middle; the equity or first-loss tranche at the bottom absorbs losses first and earns the most if things go well. Cash flows down this waterfall from the top, while losses climb up from the bottom. Thick junior tranches protect senior investors, a form of credit enhancement. The word has a second, everyday meaning: an instalment of money released over time, as when a lender or the IMF disburses a loan in tranches as conditions are met. Do not assume a senior tranche is risk-free. In 2008, many AAA tranches of mortgage CDOs suffered heavy losses because the underlying loans defaulted together.
example: Say a ₹100 crore loan pool backs a senior tranche of ₹80 crore, a mezzanine tranche of ₹15 crore and an equity tranche of ₹5 crore. If the pool loses ₹12 crore, the equity tranche is wiped out, the mezzanine loses ₹7 crore and keeps ₹8 crore, and the senior tranche is untouched.

short: A bond whose payments come from a pool of loans or receivables, such as car loans or credit card balances, not the issuer's general income.
kid: Lots of friends each owe you a little pocket money. You let another friend buy a ticket that gets paid from all those little payments as they come in.
detail: An asset-backed security (ABS) is a bond issued by a special purpose vehicle and repaid from the cash flows of a pool of assets, typically auto loans, credit card receivables, student loans, equipment leases, or consumer and microfinance loans. In US usage, ABS usually excludes mortgages, which are called MBS; in the broad sense both are ABS. The pool is often split into tranches and protected by credit enhancement, so senior notes can be rated higher than the lender that made the loans. Investors care about the pool's default, delinquency and prepayment rates more than the originator's own health. In India, ABS are mostly issued as pass-through certificates backed by vehicle, microfinance, gold or personal loans, and carry ratings with an SO (structured obligation) suffix. Do not confuse ABS with covered bonds: in a covered bond the issuing bank stays liable and keeps the assets on its balance sheet.
example: Say an ABS is backed by $500 million of car loans paying 9% a year, or $45 million in interest. The bonds total $450 million at 6%, needing $27 million. The $18 million gap, before servicing fees and losses, is a cushion called excess spread.

short: A bond backed by a pool of home or property loans, paying investors from the borrowers' monthly mortgage payments.
kid: Many families each pay a little every month for their houses. Someone collects all those little payments into one bucket and shares them with people who bought tickets.
detail: A mortgage-backed security (MBS) is a bond whose cash flows come from a pool of mortgages. Residential MBS (RMBS) are backed by home loans and commercial MBS (CMBS) by loans on offices, malls and hotels. In the US, agency MBS are guaranteed by Ginnie Mae, backed by the government, or by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, government-sponsored firms placed under federal conservatorship in 2008; they carry little default risk and form one of the world's largest bond markets. Non-agency MBS, including the subprime bonds at the centre of the 2008 crisis, carry real credit risk. The distinctive risk is prepayment: when rates fall, homeowners refinance and investors get money back just when reinvesting is least attractive, giving MBS negative convexity. The Fed bought trillions of dollars of agency MBS during quantitative easing. India's RMBS market is small; most home-loan securitisation happens through direct assignment or pass-through certificates.
example: Say a $1 billion pool of 30-year home loans at 6.5% backs an MBS paying investors 6%; the 0.5 percentage point gap covers servicing and guarantee fees. If rates fall and 10% of borrowers refinance in a year, $100 million of principal returns early, to be reinvested at lower rates.

short: In India, a security issued by a trust holding a pool of loans, passing the borrowers' repayments straight on to investors.
kid: Your friends pay you back their borrowed coins, and you hand each coin straight to the kid holding your ticket. You are just the messenger.
detail: A pass-through certificate (PTC) is the main securitisation instrument in India. A lender sells a pool of loans to a special purpose trust, which issues PTCs to investors; as borrowers pay interest and principal, the trust passes the money through to PTC holders, minus servicing fees. PTCs are often issued in senior and subordinated series, with credit enhancement such as cash collateral or over-collateralisation from the originator, and are rated with an SO (structured obligation) suffix. Buyers include banks, which can count PTCs backed by priority-sector loans towards their lending targets, and mutual funds. NBFCs and microfinance lenders use PTCs to raise funds and diversify away from bank borrowing. The alternative route is direct assignment, where the buyer purchases the loans outright with no certificate. Do not mistake a PTC for an ordinary bond: its payments depend on the loan pool, so they can arrive early or fall short.
example: Say a trust holds ₹200 crore of microfinance loans backing PTCs. In a month, borrowers repay ₹12 crore of principal and interest; after a ₹20 lakh servicing fee, ₹11.8 crore is passed through to PTC holders.

short: A security that pools many bonds or loans and slices the risk into layers, with junior layers absorbing losses first.
kid: Imagine a tower of blocks made from many friends' promises. If some promises break, the bottom blocks fall first, and the top blocks stay safe unless lots break at once.
detail: A collateralised debt obligation (CDO) is a structured product that pools debt, such as corporate bonds, loans or other asset-backed securities, and issues tranches of different seniority against it. Senior tranches are paid first and rated highest; the equity tranche takes the first losses and earns the highest yield. A synthetic CDO gains credit exposure through credit default swaps instead of owning the debt, and a CDO-squared holds tranches of other CDOs. Before 2008, CDOs packed with subprime mortgage bonds were sold with AAA ratings that assumed defaults would not cluster; when house prices fell, losses were correlated and many top-rated tranches collapsed, amplifying the crisis. Goldman Sachs paid $550 million in 2010 to settle SEC charges over its Abacus synthetic CDO. Do not lump CDOs together with CLOs: CLOs hold diversified corporate loans, are actively managed, and their senior tranches held up far better.
example: Say a $1 billion CDO has a $700 million senior tranche, a $200 million mezzanine tranche and a $100 million equity tranche. If the pool loses $250 million, the equity tranche is wiped out and the mezzanine loses $150 million. Only if losses exceed $300 million does the senior tranche lose anything.

short: A managed pool of loans to heavily indebted companies, funded by selling layered bonds to investors who take different levels of risk.
kid: A toy shop owner lends toys to many risky friends at once. He sells tickets: front-of-line tickets get paid back first, back-of-line tickets get paid last but earn extra treats.
detail: A collateralised loan obligation (CLO) is a securitisation of leveraged loans, typically 150 to 300 senior secured, floating-rate loans to sub-investment-grade companies. A CLO manager actively buys and sells loans within set limits during a reinvestment period of several years. The CLO funds itself with tranches rated from AAA down to BB, plus an equity tranche that collects whatever interest is left after the debt tranches are paid. Coverage tests divert cash away from the equity if the portfolio weakens. CLOs are the biggest buyers of US leveraged loans, so CLO demand directly shapes how cheaply private equity firms can finance buyouts. Because the loans are diversified, secured and floating-rate, CLO senior tranches came through the 2008 crisis far better than mortgage CDOs. The main confusion is treating CLOs and CDOs as the same thing; another is forgetting that equity tranche returns are highly sensitive to default rates.
example: Say a $500 million CLO buys 200 loans of $2.5 million each, funded by $450 million of rated tranches and $50 million of equity. If the loans earn 8% ($40 million a year) and the tranches cost 6.5% on average ($29.25 million), $10.75 million is left for equity before fees and losses, a 21.5% return on $50 million.

short: The recurring pattern in which lending expands and standards loosen in good times, then defaults rise and lenders pull back.
kid: When everyone is happy, kids lend toys to anyone. Then some toys don't come back, everyone gets careful and stops lending, until things feel safe again.
detail: The credit cycle is the rise and fall in the availability and price of credit. In the upswing, confident lenders cut rates and relax standards, borrowers take on more debt, asset prices climb and defaults stay low. Eventually weaker loans sour, defaults and bad loans rise, lenders tighten, credit spreads widen and borrowing shrinks, which can deepen a recession. Credit cycles often last longer than business cycles and drive banking crises; Hyman Minsky argued that long stable periods themselves breed risky lending. Regulators watch indicators such as the credit-to-GDP gap and can raise capital buffers in booms. India's last full cycle ran from the infrastructure lending boom of the late 2000s to a bad-loan peak around 2018, when banks' gross NPAs topped 11%, followed by years of clean-up. Do not confuse the credit cycle with the business cycle: they interact but do not move in lockstep.
example: Say banks' gross bad loans rise from 3% to 9% of a ₹100 lakh crore loan book during a downturn. Bad loans jump from ₹3 lakh crore to ₹9 lakh crore, and lenders respond by cutting new lending and charging riskier borrowers more.

short: A sudden sharp drop in the availability of loans, when lenders become unwilling or unable to lend even to sound borrowers.
kid: One day the toy lender gets scared and stops lending toys to anyone, even to good friends who always give them back. Suddenly nobody can borrow anything.
detail: A credit crunch is an abrupt fall in the supply of credit, usually because lenders have taken losses, are short of capital or funding, or fear that borrowers and counterparties will fail. Its signature is that even creditworthy companies cannot borrow or roll over debt on reasonable terms, so they cut spending, delay payments or sell assets, which can push the economy into recession. The 2007-08 global financial crisis was a classic crunch, as banks stopped lending to each other. In India, the default of IL&FS in September 2018 froze funding for many NBFCs, as mutual funds and banks pulled back from their commercial paper and bonds. The common confusion is with tight monetary policy: higher policy rates make credit dearer, while a crunch makes it unavailable at almost any price. Central banks usually respond with emergency liquidity rather than rate changes alone.
example: Say ABC Ltd must roll over ₹200 crore of three-month commercial paper that normally costs 8%. In a crunch, buyers demand 12%, so the extra cost is ₹200 crore x 4% x 3/12 = ₹2 crore; if no buyers turn up at all, ABC must draw on bank lines or sell assets.

short: A checklist lenders use to judge a borrower: character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions.
kid: Before lending a toy, you ask five things. Is my friend honest, can he look after it, does he have his own toys, what will he give me if he breaks it, and is today a good day to lend?
detail: The five Cs are a classic framework for judging creditworthiness. Character is the borrower's track record and honesty, judged through repayment history and credit scores such as CIBIL in India. Capacity is the ability to repay from income or cash flow, measured by ratios like debt service coverage or, for individuals, the share of income already going to EMIs. Capital is the borrower's own money in the business or purchase, which shows commitment and absorbs losses. Collateral is security the lender can claim if things go wrong. Conditions cover the loan's purpose, amount and terms as well as the economic and industry backdrop. Some texts use four Cs, dropping conditions, and others add more. Bank credit appraisals and rating agency reports are built around these ideas. The common mistake is leaning on collateral: good lenders expect repayment from cash flow, with collateral only as a backstop.
example: Say a shop owner earning ₹1.5 lakh a month, already paying ₹30,000 in EMIs, applies for a ₹20 lakh loan with a ₹40,000 EMI against a shop worth ₹30 lakh. Total EMIs would be ₹70,000, about 46.7% of income, and the loan is about 66.7% of the collateral's value. With a strong credit score, the lender may approve.

short: The risk that borrowers repay loans early, usually after rates fall, leaving lenders to reinvest the money at lower rates.
kid: You lent a friend your toy and he was giving you a sweet every day for it. Then he gives the toy back early, and the sweets stop coming.
detail: Prepayment risk is the uncertainty about when principal will come back on loans and securities that let borrowers repay early, such as home loans and mortgage-backed securities. Borrowers prepay most when rates fall, to refinance more cheaply. Investors then lose the high-coupon income they were counting on and must reinvest at lower yields; this is also called contraction risk. The mirror image is extension risk: when rates rise, prepayments slow and investors are stuck longer with below-market coupons. Together they give MBS negative convexity, meaning prices rise less when rates fall, and fall more when rates rise, than a plain bond. Investors price this with prepayment-speed models and option-adjusted spreads. In India, under the rules as of 2025, lenders cannot charge prepayment penalties on individuals' floating-rate loans taken for non-business purposes. Do not confuse it with default risk: prepayment returns all the money, just at the wrong time.
example: Say an investor holds a ₹100 crore home-loan pool yielding 9%. Rates fall and ₹20 crore is prepaid in the first year; reinvested at 7%, that slice earns ₹1.4 crore a year instead of ₹1.8 crore, a shortfall of ₹40 lakh a year.

short: When a parent company's lenders effectively rank behind its subsidiaries' lenders, because the parent only owns shares in those subsidiaries.
kid: Your big brother owns a lemonade stand, and you lent him sweets. If the stand closes, the stand's own helpers get paid first, and you only get what is left over for your brother.
detail: Structural subordination arises in group structures. If a holding company borrows but the operating assets and cash flows sit in its subsidiaries, the holding company's lenders have no direct claim on those assets. In a default, each subsidiary's own creditors, including its lenders, suppliers and employees, are paid from its assets first; only what is left flows up to the parent as a shareholder. So holdco debt ranks behind opco debt even if both are labelled senior. It is common in conglomerates, infrastructure groups and private equity structures, and rating agencies often rate holdco debt a notch or two below operating-company debt for this reason. Lenders reduce the problem with upstream guarantees from subsidiaries, share pledges or dividend and cash-sweep covenants. Do not confuse it with contractual subordination, where a bond's own terms make it junior; structural subordination comes from the corporate structure, not the contract.
example: Say HoldCo Ltd owns 100% of OpCo Ltd and has borrowed ₹300 crore. OpCo owes its own lenders ₹800 crore and its assets fetch ₹1,000 crore in liquidation. OpCo's lenders are paid ₹800 crore first, only ₹200 crore flows up to HoldCo, and HoldCo's lenders recover at most about 67%.

short: The rule that in a bankruptcy, more senior claims must be paid in full before more junior claims, and shareholders, receive anything.
kid: When a broken lemonade stand shares out its last coins, everyone stands in a line. The first kid in line gets all he is owed before the next kid gets even one coin.
detail: The absolute priority rule sets the order in which claimants are paid when an insolvent company's value is distributed: secured creditors, then senior unsecured creditors, then subordinated creditors, then preference shareholders, and finally equity shareholders. Each class must be paid in full before the next gets anything. In US Chapter 11, a plan forced on a dissenting class must respect it, though negotiated deals often give junior classes small amounts to speed things up. India's version is the Section 53 waterfall of the IBC: insolvency and liquidation costs; then workmen's dues for 24 months alongside secured creditors who give up their security; other employees' dues; unsecured financial creditors; government dues and the unpaid part of secured debts; other debts; preference shareholders; and finally equity shareholders. Resolution plans need not follow it exactly but must give certain creditors at least their liquidation entitlement. The rule explains why equity often gets nothing.
example: Say a company is liquidated for ₹500 crore after costs, owing secured lenders ₹400 crore and unsecured creditors ₹300 crore. Secured lenders are paid ₹400 crore in full, unsecured creditors share the remaining ₹100 crore for a recovery of about 33%, and shareholders receive nothing.

short: The share of loans on which borrowers have missed payments for a set period, such as 30 or 90 days.
kid: Ten friends promised to pay back one sweet each week. If two of them are late, two out of ten are behind, and you start to worry.
detail: A delinquency rate measures the proportion of loans, by value or number, that are past due, usually reported in buckets such as 30+, 60+ and 90+ days. It is an early warning signal: delinquencies rise before loans turn into defaults and write-offs. The charge-off rate is the later-stage measure, the share of loans written off as uncollectable; US banks typically charge off credit card balances after 180 days past due. In India the equivalent language is days past due: loans overdue up to 30, 31 to 60 and 61 to 90 days are classed as special mention accounts SMA-0, SMA-1 and SMA-2, and beyond 90 days a loan generally becomes a non-performing asset. Investors watch credit card, personal loan and microfinance delinquencies closely, as these turn first. The common confusion: a delinquent loan is not yet a loss. Many borrowers catch up, so delinquency and default rates differ.
example: Say ABC Finance has ₹2,000 crore of personal loans, of which ₹90 crore are 30 or more days past due. Its 30+ delinquency rate is 4.5%; if ₹30 crore of that is over 90 days overdue, 1.5% of the book is non-performing.
formula: Delinquency rate = Loans past due beyond a set number of days / Total loans outstanding x 100

short: Two classes of creditors under India's insolvency law: those who lent money, like banks, and those owed for goods, services, wages or taxes.
kid: Some friends lent you pocket money, and some gave you cookies you haven't paid for yet. Both want something back, but the friends who lent money get to decide what happens.
detail: The IBC splits creditors by the kind of debt they hold. A financial creditor is owed a financial debt, money disbursed against consideration for the time value of money: bank and NBFC loans, bonds and debentures, and, since a 2018 amendment upheld by the Supreme Court, homebuyers. An operational creditor is owed for goods or services supplied, for employment, or as dues to the government. The difference drives power in a CIRP. Financial creditors file under Section 7 by showing a default and sit on the committee of creditors with voting rights. Operational creditors file under Section 9 after a demand notice, can be blocked by a pre-existing dispute, and have no vote, though a resolution plan must pay them at least what they would get in liquidation. The common confusion is assuming suppliers or tax authorities can veto a plan; under the IBC, only financial creditors vote.
example: Say ABC Ltd owes a bank ₹600 crore, bondholders ₹200 crore and suppliers ₹100 crore. The committee of creditors holds ₹800 crore of votes, so the bank's 75% share alone clears the 66% bar to approve a plan. The suppliers get no vote, but must receive at least their liquidation value.
